turn_text: Welcome to our Brexit Watch podcast. I'll look behind the headlines after Britain's decision to leave the EU and in the immediate aftermath of that referendum, much consternation across the Atlantic in terms of how the United States economy might be affected by Britain's departure from the European Union. Britain is the biggest foreign investor in the United States, making up 15% of foreign direct investment ahead of Canada, China and Japan. And the US is the biggest export market for the UK, receiving more than $31 billion worth of British goods each year. So when President Barack Obama issued a stark warning that a UK outside the EU would go to the back of the queue in trade relations with America, alarm bells sounded, there was a feeling, especially among pro-leave politicians, that President Obama was disrespecting the special relationship in favour of cultivating ties with the leaders of Germany and France. Well, how much has changed since the election of Donald Trump and the Republican-controlled Congress? There is now considerable momentum for a US-UK bilateral trade deal. After the Brexit vote, Mr Trump had promised to strengthen our ties with a free and independent Britain, deepening our bonds in commerce, culture and mutual defence to quote him. And there are already no less than five pieces of congressional legislation calling for an Anglo-American free trade deal. most prominent being the United Kingdom Trade Continuity Act, introduced in the Senate by Mike Lee of Utah and Tom Cotton of Arkansas, both rising stars in the Republican Party. I spoke to Senator Lee about his views on how Brexit will impact Britain's relationship with the United States economy.

turn_text: First thing we can do is to continue the special relationship that has existed for more than 100 years between the United States and the United Kingdom. One that has served as the foundation for our shared pursuit of freedom, security, and democracy in the world. So that's why I've introduced the United Kingdom Trade Continuity Act, which would allow the US-UK commercial relationship to continue operating under the parameters of the current US-EU commercial agreements until a new US-UK agreement can be made.
And how would that work practically? What are the things that the two countries can trade right now and continue that relationship even after Brexit?

In the first instance, it would keep everything intact. It would make everything stand as is. And then it would also require the President of the United States to initiate negotiations within 30 days of the passage of this act to reach a new bilateral trade agreement within one year. This is important because this is a big trade relationship. You know, in 2015 alone, the United States had $56 billion worth of exports to the United Kingdom with nearly $58 billion in imports.

So that's a really important relationship for the United Kingdom and indeed the United States. And yet, President Obama said that Britain would go to the back of the queue. How likely is it that your legislation can be enacted in time to keep the relationship to remain continuous?

Let me put it this way. I know that I'm not alone when I say that this relationship is important. I know that I'm not alone in saying that President Obama's position about the United Kingdom needing to go to the back of the queue, I'm not sure what that means, but whatever it means, it should not mean that we discontinue the special relationship we have. Here's the bottom line. We are committed, and I believe others in Congress, are also committed, to making sure that we do whatever we can to work with Prime Minister Theresa May and International Trade Secretary Liam Fox to make sure that this works, to make sure that this trade relationship survives, and in fact continues to thrive, and that's exactly why I've introduced the United Kingdom Trade Continuity Act.
Why are bilateral trade deals better than multilateral trade deals, which the President-elect says in general are lousy deals?

Well, particularly when you're dealing with two significant parties like the United States and the United Kingdom. We are big players on the international trade scene. And I think that the United States in particular, regardless of who it's interacting with, has a lot of bargaining power because there are so many countries that want to trade with the United States. And to the extent we can secure better deals through bilateral agreements and to the extent that bilateral agreements enable us to avoid having to deal with an intervening multilateral international superpower, an entity to which the United States would have to yield up a certain amount of sovereignty as a condition precedent for joining a particular multilateral trade agreement, that could be an additional advantage.
Of course, until Britain leaves the EU, it's not actually in a position, at least legally, to negotiate individual trade deals.

Fair point, fair point. But that's exactly why I've written the United Kingdom Trade Continuity Act with this in mind and for that eventuality in mind. There would be no need for this bill if the Brexit had not happened. And so that's why it's with the Brexit in mind that I wrote this and that's our focus here.
